tier_reason: Shootout table on prng.di.unimi.it shows xoshiro256++ 0.75 ns/64b, 0.34 cycles/B vs MT19937-64 1.36 ns, 0.62 cycles/B. The harness (harness.c) and generator sources are public, and gcc 12.2.1 and the i7-12700KF are named. It is not A because the page never gives the optimization level (only -fno-unroll-loops) and it times the Matsumoto-Nishimura reference MT19937-64 C code, not std::mt19937_64. The peer-reviewed ACM TOMS 47(4) 2021 paper (arXiv:1805.01407, Table 1) independently shows the same win: xoshiro256++ 0.86 ns vs MT19937-64 2.19 ns (i7-8700B, gcc 8.3.0), which supports B.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc 12.2.1 with -fno-unroll-loops; -march=native deliberately not used (page: gains 'might not be possible when the generator is embedded in user code'); optimization level (-O) not stated on the page.
corrections.license: 0BSD (generator sources, e.g. xoshiro256plusplus.c, carry a public-domain dedication plus the 0BSD permission text; not CC0-1.0)
corrections.stars_or_usage: Per the page's Adoption section: default PRNG in Julia (xoshiro256++), Lua and GNU Fortran (xoshiro256**), .NET 6 (xoshiro256**/xoshiro128**); Rust rand SmallRng is xoshiro256++/xoshiro128++; Java 17 java.util.random ships xoroshiro128++/xoshiro256++; Mbed/Zephyr use xoroshiro128+. (JS engines/V8 use the older xorshift128+, and NumPy's default is PCG64, not xoshiro.)
corrections.caveats: Author-run first-party site (Sebastiano Vigna, co-author of the algorithms), not an independent benchmark. The optimization level is not stated (only -fno-unroll-loops, no -march=native). The MT19937-64 row times the Matsumoto-Nishimura reference C implementation, not std::mt19937_64 from libstdc++/libc++/MSVC STL, and the 32-bit MT19937/std::mt19937 is not in the table. Results are corroborated by the peer-reviewed ACM TOMS 47(4) 2021 paper (DOI 10.1145/3460772; arXiv:1805.01407 Table 1: xoshiro256++ 0.86 ns vs MT19937-64 2.19 ns, i7-8700B, gcc 8.3.0). harness.c is GPL-3.0-or-later (benchmark only). The generators are public domain/0BSD with no patent grant. This is a hand-maintained website, not a git repo; xoshiro256plusplus.c Last-Modified header is 2026-06-19.

notes: Numbers match this project's row. Downgraded A->B: the -O level is unstated and the named std:: baseline is not what was timed. Fixed the stars_or_usage claims about NumPy and V8 (both wrong per the page itself) and the license (text is 0BSD + public-domain dedication, not CC0).

tier_reason: NSDI'19 is peer-reviewed and third-party to RE2. Its Table 5 shows RE2-s (1,777 s / 4,696 s) beating PCRE v8.41 (6,942 s / 12,800 s) on Talos/ET-Open, with CPU, GCC 5.4 and library versions stated. No harness or artifact is public, and the traffic trace is private, so it is B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Table 5 (seconds): RE2-s beats PCRE v8.41 (JIT enabled per the paper): Talos 6942s -> 1777s (~3.9x); ET-Open 12800s -> 4696s (~2.7x) (derived from page data). RE2-s is slower than PCRE2 v10.32 JIT (1777 vs 394 s; 4696 vs 913 s). In multi-regex mode RE2-m beats serially-run PCRE2 on Talos (29 s vs 394 s, ~13.6x, derived from page data) but not on ET-Open (1116 s vs 913 s). Paper states Hyperscan-s beats RE2-s by 10.3x/9.1x.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 5.4; RE2 v2018-09-01; PCRE v8.41 and PCRE2 v10.32 with JIT enabled ('We enable the JIT option for both PCRE and PCRE2'); PCRE/PCRE2 match one regex at a time, and totals were measured serially for all engines' -s modes; optimization flags not stated.
corrections.caveats: RE2's own benchlog files (benchlog.c2/.mini/.r70/.wreck) only compare against classic PCRE on old hardware (Core2 T5600, Opteron 8214 HE, MacPro1,1), with no PCRE2 or std::regex. The only methodologically documented numbers are from the third-party NSDI'19 Hyperscan paper (written by Hyperscan developers). There, RE2 beats JIT-enabled PCRE v8.41, loses to PCRE2 JIT in single-regex mode, and beats PCRE2 only in multi-regex mode on the Talos ruleset. Separately, WG21 paper P1433R0 (by the CTRE author, no hardware/flags stated) reports RE2 3.759 s vs std::regex (libstdc++) 33.585 s and RE2 10.35 s vs std::regex (libc++) 1655 s on a ~1.3 GB CSV scan (C-level evidence). Baseline recorded is PCRE, not std::regex/PCRE2, so baseline_in_list=false.

notes: Numbers verified in Table 5. The record wrongly called PCRE 'classic (non-JIT)': the paper enabled JIT for both PCRE and PCRE2. Fixed that and added the RE2-m vs PCRE2 Talos result plus the P1433R0 std::regex datapoint. Metadata checks out: BSD-3-Clause, 9,803 stars, last commit 2026-01-22, not archived or a fork.

tier_reason: clang-bench.txt/gcc-bench.txt (committed 2018-10-23) are first-party raw `time` outputs with CTRE vs std::regex. They give no compiler version, flags, CPU or input, and ratios exceed 50x, so C. The WG21 paper P1433R0 adds stdlib names and input size but still no CPU/flags, so it stays C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: clang-bench.txt: CTRE 10.093s vs std::regex 21m9.309s (~125x, derived from page data) on 'ABCD|DEFGH|EFGHI|A{4,}'; CTRE 14.197s vs std::regex 2m34.505s (~10.9x, derived from page data) on '[0-9a-fA-F]{8,16}'; CTRE 7.596s vs std::regex 7m54.793s (~62.5x, derived from page data) on '^([0-9]{4,16})?[aA]'; CTRE 59.864s vs std::regex 27m35.004s (~27.6x, derived from page data) on the alternation pattern. gcc-bench.txt shows smaller gaps, e.g. CTRE 3.982s vs std::regex 0m55.058s (~13.8x, derived from page data) on the first pattern.
corrections.caveats: The README has no benchmark numbers, and compile-time.re/graph/ is JS-rendered. clang-bench.txt/gcc-bench.txt date from 2018-10-23 and give no compiler version, flags, CPU or input size, so they predate current v3. Benchmark sources exist in tests/benchmark-exec (ctre.cpp, std.cpp, pcre.cpp, re2.cpp, ...), and the current Makefile builds with -O3, but the txt files cannot be tied to them. WG21 P1433R0 (same author) has another first-party table on a ~1.3 GB CSV with pattern ([0-9]{4,16})?[aA]: CTRE 3.172 s vs std::regex (libstdc++) 33.585 s on GNU/gcc, and CTRE 11.11 s vs std::regex (libc++) 1655 s on macOS/clang. That 1655 s figure equals clang-bench.txt's 4th-pattern std::regex time, so data provenance is unclear. Several ratios exceed 50x with flags unstated.

notes: All numbers verified in both txt files. Ratios were unmarked, so I added '(derived from page data)'. baseline_stdlib is left [] because the benchmark_url files don't name a stdlib, but P1433R0 names libstdc++ and libc++. Metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, 3,855 stars, last commit 2026-09-11. P1433 does cite CTRE as its implementation.

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed NSDI'19 paper. Table 5 and its text give exactly the quoted times and speedups vs PCRE2 v10.32 (JIT), on a Xeon Platinum 8180 with GCC 5.4. The harness and traffic trace are not public, and the authors are Hyperscan developers, so B, not A.
notes: All Table 5 values, the quoted ratios (40.1x/10.3x/2.3x, 13.5x/183.3x, 24.8x/9.1x/1.8x, 8.4x/6.9x) and the Snort figures (113 vs 986 Mbps, 8.73x) are verified verbatim. GitHub reports license NOASSERTION, but COPYING is BSD-3-Clause and LICENSE says BSD with bundled Boost (BSL-1.0) headers, so BSD-3-Clause stands. 5,492 stars, last commit 2026-09-17. Category 'regex-engines' is inconsistent with 'regex' used elsewhere in this batch (not a correctable field).
